.²1 an inference from circumstances, presumption, implication, one of the
 five sources of knowledge or modes of proof, according to the Mīmāṃsakas.
 It is ‘deduction of a matter from that which could not else be’; it is
 ‘assumption of a thing, not itself perceived but necessarily implied by
 another which is seen, heard, or proved’; it is an inference used to account
 for an apparent inconsistency; as in the familiar instance {#pIno devadatto#}
 {#divA na BuNkte#} the apparent inconsistency between ‘fatness’ and ‘not
 eating by day’ is accounted for by the inference of his ‘eating by night’.
 {#pInatvaviSizwasya devadattasya rAtriBojitvarUpArTasya SabdAnuktasyApi#}
 {#ApattiH#}. It is defined by Śabara as {#dfzwaH Sruto vArTo'nyaTA nopapadyate#}
 {#ityarTakalpanA . yaTA jIvati devadatte gfhABAvadarSanena bahirBAvasyAdfzwasya#}
 {#kalpanA ..#} <ls>MS. 1. 1. 5</ls>. It may be seen from the words {#dfzwaH#} and
 {#SrutaH#} in the above definition, that Śabara has suggested two varieties
 of {#arTApatti#} {%<ab>viz.</ab>%} {#dfzwArTApatti#} and {#SrutArTApatti#}. The
 illustration given by him, however, is of {#dfzwArTApatti#} only. The
 former {%<ab>i. e.</ab>%} {#dfzwArTApatti#} consists in the presumption of some
 {#adfzwa arTa#} to account for some {#dfzwa arTa#} (or {#arTa#}s) which
 otherwise becomes inexplicable. The latter, on the other hand, consists
 in the presumption of some {#arTa#} through {#aSruta Sabda#} to account
 for some {#Sruta arTa#} ({%<ab>i. e.</ab>%} some statement). This peculiarity of
 {#SrutArTApatti#} is clearly stated in the following couplet; {#yatra#}
 {#tvaparipUrRasya vAkyasyAnvayasidDaye . Sabdo'DyAhriyate tatra SrutArTApattirizyate ..#}
 <ls>Mānameyodaya p. 129 (ed. by K. Raja, Adyar, 1933)</ls>. Strictly speaking
 it is no separate mode of proof; it is only a case of {#anumAna#} and
 can be proved by a {#vyatirekavyApti#}; <ab>cf.</ab> <ls>Tarka K. 17</ls> and <ls>S. D. 460</ls>.
.²2 a figure of speech (according to some rhetoricians) in which a relevant
